Family Health

Menstrual odor: normal changes and when to seek care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Periods have a smell, and a mild familiar odor is not a sign that you are unclean. Blood, uterine lining, vaginal bacteria and sweat can all contribute. A new, strong or persistent odor deserves attention, especially with pain, unusual discharge or illness; smell alone cannot identify the cause.

What can be normal during a period?

Menstrual fluid contains blood and shed uterine lining, mixed with vaginal secretions. It may smell mildly metallic or like blood, and the scent can vary through a period or between cycles. Menstruation is not a visible discharge of unfertilized eggs. Normal vaginal bacteria and changing acidity also influence odor.

There is no requirement to have no genital scent. Whether someone else notices a smell is not a reliable test of health. Compare a change with your usual pattern, but do not rely on smell to diagnose infection or to rule it out. Persistent concerns are a reasonable reason to ask for care without embarrassment.

A strong or rotten smell needs context

Blood left in a used product can develop a stronger smell. Changing the product may help, but a new persistent foul or rotten smell should not automatically be dismissed as normal menstrual tissue. Unusual discharge, soreness or pelvic pain can suggest a problem needing assessment, including a retained tampon or infection.

If you think a tampon may be forgotten, remove it promptly if it comes out easily with clean hands. Do not use tools, pull forcefully or insert another tampon. If you cannot remove it easily, are unsure one remains or think part is still inside, arrange prompt medical help. Do not wait for the period to end or for the smell to disappear.

Fishy odor and bacterial vaginosis

A fishy smell, sometimes with thin grey-white discharge, can occur with bacterial vaginosis (BV), an imbalance in vaginal bacteria. BV is not a fungal infection. Odor alone does not confirm it, and BV often causes no itching or soreness. Burning, itching, irritation or a different discharge can indicate another or an additional problem, so testing may be needed.

BV may become more noticeable around a period or after sex; menstruation is not its only cause. It can occur without sexual activity and is not proof of poor hygiene or infidelity. A clinician may examine and sample discharge to distinguish BV from sexually transmitted and other infections. Prescribed antibiotics can help, but recurrence is common; persistent or recurrent symptoms need review rather than a promise of permanent odor removal.

Sweaty, salty or onion-like changes

A sweaty, musky, salty or onion-like smell may come from the groin and external skin rather than from inside the vagina. Heat, activity, moisture and normal skin bacteria can contribute even with regular washing. These descriptions do not by themselves diagnose infection or establish that someone has neglected hygiene.

Change damp clothing and choose comfortable, breathable underwear if helpful. Cotton and other suitable fabrics may reduce trapped moisture, but they do not cure BV or another infection. Seek assessment if an unusual smell persists, worsens or comes with discharge, itching, burning or pain rather than trying to mask it.

Different products have different care instructions

Wash your hands before and after changing menstrual products. For tampons, FDA advice is to change every 4–8 hours, never exceed 8 hours and use the lowest absorbency needed for your flow. Use them only during menstruation and remove the final tampon when the period ends. Lighter bleeding is not a reason to leave one in longer; use another suitable product if needed.

Pads and period underwear collect blood outside the body; cups collect it inside. Change pads when wet or soiled and regularly according to the instructions and your flow. Follow the specific cup or disc emptying limits and cleaning instructions, and the washing and drying instructions for reusable products. Do not apply one wear time to every product. Pain, irritation or unusual symptoms warrant stopping the troublesome product and seeking advice.

Gentle care without deodorizing the vagina

Gently wash the outside genital skin, the vulva, with warm water; a mild unperfumed soap may be used if tolerated. Routine bathing and changing products can improve comfort, but repeated scrubbing or internal washing is unnecessary. The vagina cleans itself; do not douche or insert antiseptics, scented wipes, sprays or deodorants to eliminate its natural scent.

Scented tampons, pads or washes can irritate some people; choose unscented options if irritation occurs. A fragrance-free routine does not guarantee an absence of odor or replace treatment. Do not self-treat a fishy smell as thrush or use leftover antibiotics. The right approach depends on the cause, not on trying to achieve a perfume-like smell.

When to book care and what assessment may involve

Arrange assessment for a new persistent fishy or foul odor, yellow or green discharge, itching, urinary burning, bleeding between periods or after sex, or bleeding or cramps different from your usual pattern. A primary care clinician or sexual health clinic can help; not every concern requires a gynecologist first. Possible pregnancy should be mentioned because bleeding is not always a period.

Seek urgent same-day advice for pelvic or lower abdominal pain with unusual discharge, fever or possible pregnancy. Evaluation may include symptom and product history, an examination with consent, swabs or a pregnancy test. Conditions such as PID need early treatment. You can ask questions, request a chaperone and stop an examination. Do not delay because you feel ashamed of a smell.

Warning signs that need immediate help

With a retained tampon or other vaginal object, fever of 38°C or higher, rash, dizziness, confusion, breathing difficulty, muscle aches or diarrhea need emergency assessment. Sudden fever, vomiting, diarrhea, rash or feeling faint during or shortly after tampon or cup use can signal rare but life-threatening toxic shock syndrome. Seek immediate medical help; remove the product if easily possible, but do not delay help or wait for every symptom. An odor is not required.

Get immediate emergency care for severe or worsening pelvic pain, sudden intense abdominal pain, pelvic pain with heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion, breathing difficulty or feeling severely unwell. If pregnancy is possible, pain with bleeding needs urgent advice even without a positive test; severe pain, shoulder-tip pain with bleeding or fainting are emergency warning signs. An app prediction that it is your period must not delay care.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current clinical advice distinguishes mild familiar odor from persistent unusual odor; symptoms and testing matter more than an odor label. BV is a bacterial imbalance and may recur after treatment.

FDA product advice specifies tampon changes every 4–8 hours with an 8-hour maximum. Pads, cups and reusable products require their own label and cleaning instructions.

Healthdirect and NHS guidance identify retained-object illness and toxic shock warning signs. Prompt removal must not delay urgent or emergency assessment; there is no need to wait for all signs or for odor.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record your usual cycle pattern, product use and changes to discuss with a clinician. It cannot identify infection or a retained tampon from odor, assess bleeding safety or exclude pregnancy. Symptoms take priority over cycle predictions and reminders.

When to seek help

Seek emergency assessment for a retained vaginal object with fever of 38°C or higher or systemic symptoms. Get immediate help for possible toxic shock, severe or worsening pelvic pain, pelvic pain with heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty. Pelvic pain with unusual discharge, fever or possible pregnancy needs urgent same-day advice. Remove an internal product only if easy; do not delay help.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Mild familiar menstrual odor, including a metallic smell, can be normal and is not a cleanliness judgment.
  • New persistent fishy or rotten odor needs assessment; smell alone cannot diagnose BV, an STI or a retained tampon.
  • Follow each product’s instructions. Tampons must never stay in longer than 8 hours; other products have their own care requirements.
  • Avoid internal washing and deodorants. Urgent illness, retained-product warning signs or severe pain need prompt or emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

Is a rotten smell during a period normal?

A used product can smell stronger, but a new persistent rotten smell should not receive blanket reassurance. Consider a forgotten tampon and seek assessment if the smell persists or comes with unusual discharge, pain or illness. A retained product should be removed promptly and safely.

Is a fishy smell just part of menstruation?

It can occur with BV or other conditions and should not be diagnosed by smell alone. BV is a bacterial imbalance, not a fungal infection or proof of poor hygiene. A clinician can check the cause and prescribe treatment when needed.

How can I reduce menstrual odor safely?

Change products as directed, gently wash the external vulva and change damp clothes if needed. Avoid douching, fragrances and internal antiseptics. Breathable underwear may help comfort but does not treat infection. Persistent odor needs assessment rather than masking.

When should I see a clinician?

Book care for a new persistent odor or unusual discharge, itching, urinary burning or abnormal bleeding. Pelvic pain with discharge, fever or possible pregnancy needs urgent same-day advice. Severe pain, heavy bleeding with pelvic pain, fainting or severe illness needs immediate emergency care.

How long can I leave a tampon in?

FDA advice is to change it every 4–8 hours and never exceed 8 hours. Choose the lowest absorbency needed, follow the label and use only during a period. Lighter flow does not justify longer use. Pads, cups and reusable products have different instructions.

What if I cannot find or remove a tampon?

If it comes out easily with clean hands, remove it promptly. Do not use tools or force. If you are unsure whether one remains, cannot remove it easily or suspect a piece remains, get prompt medical help. Fever or systemic symptoms with a retained object need emergency assessment.

Does a sweaty or onion-like smell mean I am dirty?

No. External sweat, moisture and normal skin bacteria can produce these smells despite regular washing. Gentle care may improve comfort. Persistent changes or additional symptoms should be assessed without blame.

Can toxic shock syndrome happen without a bad smell?

Yes. Odor is not required. Sudden fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness or feeling faint during or shortly after tampon or cup use need immediate medical help. Remove the product if easy, but do not delay care or wait for every symptom.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
